# Workflow Triggers & Operational Behaviour

## 1. Command Reference

The commands and skills are provided by the `mayker-dev` plugin; they are not files in this repo. Once the plugin is installed, commands are available namespaced as `/mayker-dev:<command>`, and each invokes the matching skill of the same name. The skill holds the full multi-phase procedure and also auto-loads by its description (including in Claude Code on the web and Routines).

| Command | Skill | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/mayker-dev:init-project [existing \| new]` | init-project | One-time project setup, part 1: generate `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/settings.json`, materialize the always-on rules, add the framework `.gitignore` entries (local, interactive) |
| `/mayker-dev:sync-project` | sync-project | Project setup part 2, and the repeatable half: MCP pre-flight, tracker status mapping, backlog import, dependency graph, `feature_map.md`, `project_state.json`, CI pipelines, project docs. Re-run whenever the tracker or the codebase moves (local, interactive) |
| `/mayker-dev:upgrade-project [--dry-run]` | upgrade-project | Carry an installed plugin update into this repo's materialized files: re-materialize the seven always-on standards, then apply the plugin's migration ledger. No checkpoints, safe anywhere |
| `/mayker-dev:plan-feature {ID}` | plan-feature | Generate an architect plan for one work item |
| `/mayker-dev:build-feature {ID}` | build-feature | Implement one work item from an approved plan |
| `/mayker-dev:plan-features {IDs \| ready \| wave N}` | plan-features | Batch: plan several items at once, one worktree and one draft plan PR each. `wave N` takes one authored front |
| `/mayker-dev:build-features {IDs \| ready \| wave N}` | build-features | Batch: build several approved items at once, one worktree and one PR each. `wave N` takes one authored front |
| `/mayker-dev:revise-feature {ID}` | revise-feature | Apply a revision based on PR review comments |
| `/mayker-dev:watch-pr [{ID \| PR}]` | watch-pr | Watch a PR's CI checks to completion and fix failures (runs at the tail of build/revise/fix/refactor/generate-tests; standalone after e.g. a re-plan) |
| `/mayker-dev:refactor frontend\|backend\|{ID} [--no-watch]` | refactor | Standalone code-quality scan and refactoring |
| `/mayker-dev:generate-tests {scope} [--tier] [--no-watch]` | generate-tests | Generate tests for a work item, module, or scope |
| `/mayker-dev:diagnose {scope}` | diagnose | Scan existing code for bugs, perf, and risks; write local work items |
| `/mayker-dev:fix {ID \| description}` | fix | Condensed plan+build for one work item, keeping the gates |
| `/mayker-dev:security-scan {scope}` | security-scan | Run an Aikido scan locally (no repo or CI required); route findings to `/fix` |
| `/mayker-dev:security-fix [findings-file]` | security-fix | Autonomously remediate Aikido findings on the current PR branch, keeping all quality gates |
| `/mayker-dev:waves [wave N]` | waves | Print the grouped wave overview of `feature_map.md`: which items form each front, their flags and status, and what is still unwaved. Read-only, writes nothing |
| `/mayker-dev:deliver [IDs]` | deliver | Autonomous mode only: drive the whole backlog to Done on the dependency graph, no human gates (`autonomy.md`) |

Follow the invoked skill's instructions exactly.

**The two batch commands are the single-item ones, N at a time.** `/plan-features` and `/build-features` run the `plan-feature` / `build-feature` procedure per selected item, each item in its own worktree, with every human gate of assisted mode intact: a plan batch ends at draft plan PRs (no plan is self-approved), a build batch ends at PRs handed over for review (nothing is merged). Their shared half — selection and the `ready` selector, refusals, conflict serialization, mandatory worktrees, the round loop, and the report — is defined once in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/batch_dispatch.md`, an on-demand standard those two skills read at Load Context. Bulk delivery *with* self-approval and merging remains `/deliver` alone.

## 2. Subagents

The plan / build / review split is expressed with dedicated subagents provided by the plugin (`planner`, `builder`, `reviewer`). The skills delegate to them by name:

| Subagent | Role | Permissions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `planner` | Architect plans (used by `/plan-feature`, `/plan-features`, `/deliver`) | Read-mostly; writes only plan artifacts under `.claude/artifacts/` |
| `builder` | Implementation + tests, and CI-failure fixes (used by `/build-feature`, `/build-features`, `/revise-feature`, `/fix`, `/watch-pr`, `/deliver`) | Read/write code, run tests, commit and push |
| `reviewer` | Self-review against `review_standards.md`, and a second narrowed pass over what that review could not cover: in `/build-feature` the UAT and documentation artifacts generated after it plus any file the refactor gate added (Phase H), and in `/deliver` 6.5, `/fix` and `/security-fix` the gate's added files alone, dispatched only when it added a source or test file (`review_standards.md` Section 6.4) — used by `/build-feature`, `/build-features`, `/fix`, `/security-fix`, `/deliver` | Read-only; cannot edit, run, or commit |
| `orchestrator` | Autonomous scheduling and verdicts (used by `/deliver`): dependency graph, readiness, conflict serialization, plan self-approval, merge decisions, run report | Read-mostly; writes only run artifacts and decision logs; spawns nothing (the main session dispatches per its decisions) |

The reviewer is intentionally read-only so it cannot quietly fix what it is meant to critique. It reports findings back; the builder applies the fixes. Because it cannot execute anything, every dispatch also hands it the run's observed test results (`.claude/artifacts/run/handover/{ID}-run.md`, build-feature's Phase dispatch note) together with the run id that says which of that record's lines are this run's, so a claim about run-time behaviour is graded against what the build actually saw: a prediction contradicting an observed pass is explained or downgraded, never BLOCKING, and a suspicion it cannot settle from reading belongs at RECOMMENDED with the command that would settle it (`review_standards.md` Sections 4 and 6.1). The orchestrator is likewise decision-only: it cannot write code, push, or merge; the main `/deliver` session executes its verdicts, which keeps the decision record and the actions auditable separately.

**No `model` argument on a dispatch.** Spawn every subagent with **no** `model` argument on the Agent/Task call. A per-invocation `model` outranks the agent definition's own `model:` pin, so passing one silently runs that step on a tier nothing chose: nothing refuses it, the run reports success, and the mandated planning or review tier simply did not happen. The tier is `agents/*.md`'s, and only `agents/*.md`'s.

### 2.1 Coordination timers and polling (the waiting policy)

This section is the single home of the delay policy for waiting on background subagents and external state. Skills and dispatching sessions reference it; never hardcode per-call delay literals in a skill step, a dispatch, or a wakeup prompt.

- **One idempotent fallback wakeup per background dispatch.** When a long-running subagent is dispatched in the background, schedule exactly one fallback wakeup at roughly 2x the expected duration of that phase (estimate from the item's scope, or from per-step statistics of earlier runs when available; never copy a fixed literal between dispatches). **Per dispatch means per dispatch, and a build is many:** each implementation phase is its own `builder` dispatch (build-feature's Phase dispatch note), so one item's build carries roughly six sized wakeups rather than one, and a batch multiplies that by the items in flight. That is the reason the sizing rule is written as an estimate per phase and not as a constant. The wakeup prompt MUST begin with this self-check, verbatim apart from the identifier: "If task {TASK_ID} already reported completion, stop this schedule (ScheduleWakeup stop) and end the turn." A stale wakeup then costs one tool call, never a re-read or re-reasoning of work that already completed.
- **Cancel on notification.** When a task notification arrives (completion or failure), the first action, before reading the result, updating any state, or dispatching the next step, is stopping every outstanding fallback timer that guarded that task. No fallback may outlive the completion it guards.
- **Adaptive polling for external state.** Waiting on state that sends no notification (CI checks, tracker transitions) never uses one long fixed timer sized to the worst case. Poll with short exponential backoff: first poll after 30 seconds, then multiply the delay by 1.5 per poll, capped at 2 minutes between polls. The calling skill sets the overall budget (for CI, 45 minutes per push: deliver Section 6.7 and the watch-pr skill Section 2) and treats exhaustion as failure. This bounds the reaction lag to at most one backoff step, so a settled result is acted on within about 2 minutes, instead of the remainder of a worst-case timer.

## 3. Operational Behaviour

- **No TODO placeholders:** Do not generate code with "TODO: Implement logic" or similar. Write the full implementation.
- **Response format:** Be concise. Use Markdown for all code blocks.
- **MCP:** The issue tracker MCP is required only when Work Item Source is `tracker` or `hybrid`; `local` source needs no tracker (see `work_items.md` and `mcp_integration.md`). The **Git provider path is keyed on the provider**: `github` is the `gh` CLI (always, in both modes, with no `mcp__github__*` call), while `gitlab` and `bitbucket` use that provider's MCP. Each skill verifies what it needs at startup — functionally, reusing the working path recorded in `project_state.json` → `git_provider.effective_path` (`mcp_integration.md` Section 5.0).
- **Config required:** The pipeline commands (`/plan-feature`, `/build-feature`, `/plan-features`, `/build-features`, `/revise-feature`, `/refactor`, `/generate-tests`) require `.claude/project_state.json` to exist. If missing, stop: "Run /sync-project first to generate .claude/project_state.json." `/diagnose`, `/fix`, `/watch-pr`, `/security-scan`, `/security-fix` and `/waves` are the six exceptions and do not require it — seven required plus six exceptions plus the four that generate, precede or report on the file (`/sync-project`, `/init-project`, `/upgrade-project`, `/deliver`) accounts for all seventeen commands, and `mcp_integration.md` Section 0 states the same seven and six. `/sync-project` generates it, `/init-project` runs before it exists and never reads it, and `/upgrade-project` reports its absence rather than stopping.
- **Autonomy compatible:** All commands except the two setup commands, `/init-project` and `/sync-project`, are designed to run autonomously without human interaction during execution. Checkpoints that require human input exist only in those two (both are run in a local, interactive Claude Code session; `/sync-project` holds all the approval stops, `/init-project` holds none but is still interactive by design). Fully unattended surfaces (Routines, GitHub Actions, headless `claude -p`) cannot answer interactive prompts, do not run either one there. **`/upgrade-project` is the maintenance path that is safe there**: it never prompts, never applies a `manual` migration, and never replaces a file, which is what makes it usable on an unattended surface where a `/sync-project` re-run is not (it runs `/init-project` Section R as its migration zero, which is where the retired `refresh-rules` sub-run's behaviour lives). **That safety is about checkpoints, not about writes.** Migration zero writes into `.claude/rules/`, and an unattended session has its `<project>/.claude/**` writes auto-declined by the CLI, above `.claude/settings.json`, `--allowedTools` and every PreToolUse hook — so a repo whose rules are **already current** upgrades there normally, and a **stale** one stops with the interactive remedy instead of reporting success (`/init-project` Section R step 4). Do not answer that stop with a permission grant, a hook `allow`, or a write routed around the refusal: none of them reaches the check, and the last one forges the stamp that is the repo's only drift signal. **On an unattended surface, name the command in its namespaced form, `/mayker-dev:<command>`:** the bare `/<command>` spelling resolves only in an interactive session, and `claude -p` answers an unknown command by printing `Unknown command` and exiting **0**, so an unattended caller must check the run's own recorded product, the artifact or the report header its instruction names, and never the exit code alone.
- **Keeping a repo current after a plugin update:** `claude plugin update` refreshes the plugin's own skills, commands, hooks and agents and refreshes **nothing the plugin materialized into the repo**. Two commands cover the rest and they are complementary, not alternatives. `/upgrade-project` carries plugin changes into the files no re-run heals (`CLAUDE.md`, the CI workflows, the `feature_map.md` structure) via the plugin's `migrations/` ledger, and re-stamps `.claude/rules/`. A `/sync-project` re-run regenerates `.claude/project_state.json` and the project docs, and `/init-project` re-appends any missing `.gitignore` entry and fills an absent `.claude/settings.json` — **and, because the boundary is per artifact rather than per file, `/sync-project` is also the only thing that heals two blocks inside `CLAUDE.md`: Backing Services (re-derived in full every time) and a `Test gate command:` that is missing or `auto`.** Every other field in `CLAUDE.md` reaches an existing repo through the ledger. `/upgrade-project`'s report names both classes and tells you when the second one is stale, so a clean migration list never reads as "fully current".
- **Autonomy mode:** the `CLAUDE.md` → Autonomy toggle selects the operating model. `assisted` (default): humans review plan PRs, set Ready for Build, review and merge implementation PRs; one command per item, or one batch command for several items (`/plan-features`, `/build-features`), which changes how many items a session moves and nothing about who approves. `autonomous`: `/deliver` drives the whole backlog per `autonomy.md`, self-approves plans, monitors and fixes CI, handles review comments, and merges by its own verdict; `/deliver` hard-stops unless the toggle reads `autonomous`, so enabling autonomy is a reviewed, committed change. Quality gates are identical in both modes.
- **Permissions:** Autonomous runs rely on the permission posture in `.claude/settings.json` so agents do not block on approvals. See `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` → Permissions & Autonomy.

## 4. Git Conventions

- **Branching:** One branch per work item, prefix `feature/`. The branch name is defined in `feature_map.md` (tracker features) or in the work item's frontmatter (local `docs/issues/` items). The standalone `/refactor` and `/generate-tests` commands instead use `refactor/` and `test/` branches respectively (they are not auto-Done work items), and the two maintenance commands `/upgrade-project` and `/sync-project` land their own generated artifacts on `chore/mayker-{command}-...` (MDF-164), as does `/deliver` for every landing it makes on the default branch that is not an item's own pull request — its initialization, a CI bootstrap, a local Done flip and the run report, on `chore/mayker-deliver-{run_id}-{purpose}` (MDF-176, deliver Section L). The `branch-guard.sh` hook allows those prefixes plus the base branches (`main`/`master`/`develop`) and blocks any other branch — including any `chore/` name outside the `mayker-` namespace, which is deliberate: a maintenance branch is allowed because a framework command generates it to a fixed pattern and opens a reviewable pull request for it, not because `chore` is a word.
- **Commits:** Use semantic commit messages:
  - `feat({FEATURE_ID}): ...` for new features
  - `fix({FEATURE_ID}): ...` for bug fixes
  - `refactor({FEATURE_ID}): ...` for code-quality improvements
  - `test({FEATURE_ID}): ...` for test additions
  - `plan({FEATURE_ID}): ...` for architect plans
  - `chore: ...` for maintenance
- **Source of truth:** Git is the master record. Never rely on local IDE history as the final state.
- **Worktrees:** `/deliver` always isolates concurrent items in per-item worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/{ID}` (gitignored, removed after merge); remote operations from any worktree go through the Git provider working path and nothing else — on a GitHub project that is `git -C <worktree> push` plus `gh` (`mcp_integration.md` Section 7). The assisted batch commands (`/plan-features`, `/build-features`) likewise always isolate, for the same reason. The single-item assisted commands do so when `CLAUDE.md` → Worktrees is `per-feature`, per Section 4.1 below.

### 4.1 Worktrees, the `Worktrees` toggle

`CLAUDE.md` → **Worktrees** decides where the assisted commands do their work. `/plan-feature`, `/build-feature`, `/revise-feature` and `/fix` all read it; `/deliver` ignores it and always uses per-item worktrees (`autonomy.md` Section 6), because parallel items cannot share a checkout. The batch commands `/plan-features` and `/build-features` ignore it for that same reason (`batch_dispatch.md` Section 4), including for a batch of one, so batch behaviour does not change with the size of the selection. Nothing about this is prompt-driven: the toggle is the only input, and a phrase in the user's message never turns it on or off.

- **`off`** — assume this when `CLAUDE.md` is absent or carries no Worktrees line: the command checks the feature branch out in the primary working copy. The original behaviour, unchanged in every detail.
- **`per-feature`** — the item's work happens in a git worktree at `.claude/worktrees/{ID}` (gitignored), created on first use and **reused** by every later command for that item.

Setup procedure, run once per command — once **per item** in a batch — right after the branch name is resolved and before anything is written:

1. Read the toggle. `off` → work in the primary checkout and skip the rest of this section. A batch run and an autonomous run skip this step entirely and always continue with step 2: the toggle does not apply to them.
2. Run `git worktree list --porcelain`. If a worktree is already checked out on `{branch}`, use **that** path, whatever it is named, and skip to step 5. Never create a second worktree for a branch, and never `git checkout` a branch another worktree holds: git refuses, and retrying around that refusal is worse than the problem it signals.
3. Otherwise create it:
   - **Branch exists** (locally or on the remote): `git fetch origin {branch}` when it is remote, then `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/{ID} {branch}`.
   - **Branch does not exist yet** (a fresh `/plan-feature` or `/fix`): `git fetch origin main` then `git worktree add -b {branch} --no-track .claude/worktrees/{ID} origin/main`. `--no-track` is mandatory for the same reason as on `git checkout -B`: the branch must never track `origin/main`, or a "Sync" push lands feature commits on main.
   - **`.claude/worktrees/{ID}` exists as a directory git does not know about** (a worktree removed by hand, or a copy): run `git worktree prune` once and retry. If the directory survives that, **STOP** and report the path. Never delete it: it may hold uncommitted work.
   - **`git worktree` is unavailable** (git older than 2.5) or the add fails for any other reason: fall back to the `off` behaviour for this run and say so in the summary. A missing worktree never blocks the lifecycle.
4. If this run has **already committed** work on the current branch of the primary checkout, finish it there and do not move to a worktree mid-run; note it in the summary. Moving would strand those commits.
5. From here on the worktree is the working directory: `cd` into it once, or prefix each command with `git -C {worktree}`. Read and write the item's files under that path — including `.claude/artifacts/{ID}/`, which is branch content — and run the tests there. The primary checkout keeps whatever branch it was on and is not touched.
6. The upstream assertion (`git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/{branch} {branch}` then `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref {branch}@{upstream}`, MUST print `origin/{branch}`) runs **in the worktree**, unchanged.
7. **Point the statistics collector at the worktree.** The step markers land in the worktree's `.claude/artifacts/{ID}/stats.jsonl`, so the in-session run at each skill's Summary must name it: `bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/stats-collect.sh --project {worktree}`. The session's `.claude/artifacts/run/session.json` may only exist in the primary checkout; when it does, pass its `transcript_path` too (`--transcript {path}`), otherwise the collector cannot resolve a transcript and reports the token metrics as ABSENT with a `**Degraded:**` line naming the cause, rather than writing zeros that read like a measurement. Statistics never block a run either way.
8. Report the worktree path in the command's summary, so the developer knows where the code is.

Removal is manual in assisted mode, since the human merges the PR: `git worktree remove .claude/worktrees/{ID}` after the merge (`git worktree prune` clears entries whose directory is already gone). A leftover worktree is harmless, the item's next command reuses it.

The deterministic hooks follow the work rather than the primary checkout: the branch guard judges the branch of the tree the commit or push actually runs in, and the test gate runs the suites in that same tree, on every `git push` spelling alike, the `git -C <dir> push` an autonomous run uses included (`hooks/branch-guard.sh`, `hooks/test-gate.sh`, both via `hooks/lib/worktree-resolve.sh`). That tree is resolved from the session **before** the command is inspected, so `git commit`, `cd <dir> && git commit` and `git -C <dir> commit` issued from one directory get one verdict — a gate whose answer changed with the spelling would teach that re-spelling the command is the way past it. Both hooks still fail open on anything they cannot resolve, and both now **say so on stderr** when they do: a fail-open that exits 0 without a word is indistinguishable from a gate that ran and passed, so treat a `[branch-guard] fail-open:` or `[test-gate] fail-open:` line as "this gate did not run", not as noise. The test gate also **exports that run's resolved backing services** before it runs the suites — the `- env:` lines of `.claude/artifacts/run/handover/{ID}-run.md`, which the build's dispatches already read instead of rediscovering the environment — so a suite whose service came up on a host-assigned port reaches it at push time too. That path is fail-open in the same way: no record changes nothing, and a record line the hook cannot use is named on stderr while the suites still run. **What it runs is scopable, and off by default.** With `CLAUDE.md` → Test Configuration → `Scoped test command:` set, a push on a `feature/{ID}-{slug}` branch runs that command against the test files of that item plus every item that depends on it and every item flagged as sharing files with one of those, resolved from `feature_map.md` by `hooks/lib/test-scope.sh`; with the line `auto`, `none` or absent it runs the full suite exactly as before. Read the gate's `precedence:` and `Scope:` lines before reading its verdict: `Scope: scoped` means the run covered this item's blast radius and **not** the repo, so CI stays the authority (`testing_standards.md` Section 2.1), and every case the resolver cannot settle falls back to the full suite with the reason named — a partial scope would pass and look complete.

## 5. Bash command shape

**One Bash call per exec turn where the work allows it, and a shape the permission layer can grant.** The batching mandate (ADR 0006: chain independent work onto one call instead of spending a round trip per command) is sound and its saving is measured. What was missing until 0.3.138 is a statement of the **shape** it must produce, so a command that batches correctly is not then refused by the layer that decides whether it may run at all. Measured on CLI 2.1.260 and re-confirmed on 2.1.263 against the shipped `templates/settings.json`: 31 of the 43 distinct Bash commands one `/plan-feature` + `/build-feature` lifecycle emitted carried at least one blocker, and the two largest could not be fixed by any allow-list entry.

**A refused command does not fail loudly.** On an attended surface it costs an approval click; on an unattended one (`/deliver`, a Routine, a GitHub Action, a cloud dispatch) there is nobody to prompt, so the call is simply not made and the step is silently unperformed. Treat a shape rule below as a correctness rule, not a tidiness rule.

### 5.1 Never emit these shapes

Each one is measured, and the first two cannot be granted by any **prefix** rule. The one rule form that does grant them is the bare tool name `Bash`, and the framework declines to ship it for the measured reasons in **5.5** — so treat all six as ungrantable in practice, and read 5.5 before proposing the escape:

- **No `$(…)` command substitution in a model-emitted command.** A command the permission analysis cannot parse prompts instead of matching a rule, and a substitution is unparseable by construction: `echo $(pwd)` and `git diff --stat $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main) HEAD` are both refused although `echo`, `pwd`, `git` and `git merge-base` are all granted. 27 of 43 commands (63%). **A value the command would substitute comes from one of exactly two places:** (1) the **printed output of a prior call in the same batch chain** — chain the producer onto the call you are already making (`… && echo done; date +%s`) and use the integer it printed as a **literal** in the next call, which costs no extra turn; or (2) a **helper script that computes it internally** and is invoked by name. Backticks are the same defect spelled differently.
- **No `.` or `source` of a script, and no `eval`.** Both are shell builtins that the permission layer refuses outright, and **no prefix rule grants either**: `Bash(source:*)`, `Bash(.:*)` and `Bash(eval:*)` were each measured to change nothing. A shared shell library is therefore reached by **running** it (`bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/<script>.sh …`), never by sourcing it into the session's shell.
- **No `cd` as a segment**, before `git` or before anything else. `cd backend && git status`, `cd backend && ls` and `cd .claude && ls` are all refused, including the read-only tails, and the published rule that a `cd` inside the working directory composes does not hold in practice (reported upstream 2026-09-08). Use `git -C <dir> …`, an explicit path argument, or a tool flag that takes a root.
- **No path that resolves outside the working directories.** The plugin cache is covered — `templates/settings.json` ships **two** `permissions.additionalDirectories` entries for it, `~/.claude/plugins/cache/mayker/mayker-dev` and `~/.mayker/mayker-dev`, and it takes both to cover it on every host. The first is version-independent because each installed version is a directory *inside* it, so `claude plugin update` does not stale it; it names the **default** config directory, and a host running a non-default `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` loads the plugin from somewhere else entirely, where that entry covers nothing (measured, and it is why the second entry exists — see 5.8) — but nothing else is. `/tmp`, a sibling checkout and a home-directory path outside that cache are all refused. **`permissions.additionalDirectories` is the only mechanism that re-opens a path, and one documented setting silently disables it: see 5.6.** **Running a program and reading a file are fenced differently, and the check RESOLVES a symlink**, measured 2026-09-10, one variable per row (MDF-195 rows `W02`, `Y01`, `Y02`, `Y03`, `Z01`). `bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/run-dir.sh …` is **allowed** with its bytes landing even though that path is in **no** `additionalDirectories` entry, so a program argument is not path-fenced. A **read** is: `grep '"version"' ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` is **DENIED** when the pointer's target sits outside every entry (`Y01`) and **allowed** when the same shape's target sits inside the shipped plugin-cache entry (`Z01`), which is the pair that shows the check judging the **resolved target** rather than the literal path. So a Bash read through the pointer works exactly where the real plugin cache is covered, and the shipped entry is what covers it.
- **No quoted string containing `git push`.** The analysis matches the substring rather than the parsed segment, so `grep -nE 'token|git push|skip ci' README.md` is refused as a push. The same substring rule makes the framework's own two push hooks fire on such a command; spell the pattern so it cannot contain the phrase.
- **No `${…}` brace expansion, and no variable the analysis cannot resolve.** Measured 2026-09-10 on CLI 2.1.267, one variable per row against the same file: `bash "$HOME/…/run-dir.sh" …` **allowed** and `bash "${HOME}/…/run-dir.sh" …` **DENIED**, so the brace form alone decides it; and `bash "$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT/…"` **DENIED** unbraced, so an unresolvable name decides it too, with the CLI's own value for the plugin it loaded and no override in play (MDF-195 row `W03`, pairing with MDF-194's `S03` on the brace form alone). The two are independent, and until 0.3.165 **every plugin-script call this framework shipped failed both**: the placeholder spelling is DENIED with the command verbatim in the denial, `cat` of the same path is refused identically so it is not about `bash`, and a session emits that literal **even when the Skill launcher has just handed it the resolved plugin root** (MDF-195 row `W07`, which is the in-situ row the forced fixtures could not give). **Name a plugin script through the pointer instead: `bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/<script>.sh …`, unquoted. Read 5.7 before you write one.**
- **No trailing `&&` or `||`**, and **no command over 10,000 characters**. Both are documented as unparseable, so both prompt.

### 5.2 What composes fine, and must not be "fixed"

Measured allowed, so a session that re-spells one of these is adding work and losing the batching saving: pipes of two and three segments; `&&`, `||` and `;` chains; `2>&1`; a quoted `--jq` filter containing `{}` or `[]`; a bare assignment segment (`M=./x; git status`); a variable redirect target that resolves inside the working directory (`echo hi >> "$M"`); **unbraced** variable expansion inside a path, where the variable is one the analysis can resolve (`cat "$PWD/.claude/project_state.json"`, `bash "$HOME/…"`) and a literal, **unquoted** `~/…` path, which is how every plugin script is named (5.7), and quoting it kills it because the shell does not expand a tilde inside quotes; an absolute path that resolves inside the repository; and `gh api`. **A prefix rule DOES compose across a compound command** — the rule is that *every* segment must match a rule independently, so a chain prompts when one segment's program has no grant, never because it is a chain.

### 5.3 One refusal no shipped settings entry reaches

**A Bash output redirection into `.claude/` is refused as a sensitive-file write, and no entry this framework ships changes that.** Measured with every `deny` rule removed and with `Edit(./.claude/**)` explicitly granted: `echo '…' >> .claude/artifacts/{ID}/stats.jsonl` is still refused. So the mandated step-marker idiom does not land on an unattended surface, whatever its shape, and a run that looks healthy produces no statistics. Do not attempt to grant your way past it, do not re-spell the command, and do not fall back to a route that hides the failure — the write is either performed by a hook or script (which the permission layer never sees) or the step is reported as unmeasured.

**That last clause is now the shipped mechanism for the step markers, and it is measured rather than inferred.** The permission layer adjudicates the **invocation** of a script and nothing the script then does, so since 0.3.161 (MDF-186) every step marker is appended by `hooks/lib/run-dir.sh` itself: `bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/run-dir.sh mark-item .claude/artifacts/{UNIT} '{json}' '{json}'` for a work-item unit, `mark-run` for a machine-local one. Measured 2026-09-09 on CLI 2.1.266 in a trusted throwaway clone under this template verbatim, one variable per row, verdicts from `permission_denials` and the file system: `echo 'x' >> .claude/artifacts/<unit>/stats.jsonl` **DENIED** with the fixture command verbatim in the denial, the equivalent `bash <script> <dir> <json> <json>` **allowed**, and both marker lines present on disk afterwards (`ticket-notes.md` `MEASURE-34`, rows H01/H05/H06). **The session still authors every marker** — it calls a script instead of emitting `echo >>`, and no hook and no dispatch writes one (`MARKERS-01`). Nothing about the write TARGET changed: `.claude/artifacts/{UNIT}/stats.jsonl` is where the collector and the hooks look, and relocating it was priced against this and rejected. **Since 0.3.163 (MDF-192) the same entry point writes a second artifact by the same route**, `/deliver`'s unattended run record: `bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/run-dir.sh run-record .claude/artifacts/run/deliver-run.json {run id} running|complete|blocked`. It is what a headless caller of that command reads instead of its closing prose line, because `claude -p` prints the assistant's final message and an unattended check reads an artifact a script wrote (`REPO-50`). Two artifacts, one route, and the route is the measured part.

**Since 0.3.164 (MDF-194) the same entry point carries a DOCUMENT as well as a line.** A step marker is one short JSON object that fits in argv; a plan, a run report, a dependency graph or a decision log is a multi-kilobyte document the model composes, so four further subcommands take the content on **stdin**: `write-item` / `append-item` for a work-item unit and `write-run` / `append-run` for a machine-local one, with the kind named by the caller and never derived (`MARKERS-08`). The caller emits a **quoted** heredoc — `<<'MAYKER_ARTIFACT'`, never the unquoted form — so a `$` in the document is not expanded. Measured 2026-09-10 on CLI 2.1.267 in a trusted clone under this template verbatim, one variable per row, verdicts from `permission_denials` and the file system: the **`Write` tool** to `.claude/artifacts/{ID}/plan.md` **DENIED** and absent, the **`Write` tool** to `.claude/artifacts/run/report.md` **DENIED** and absent, the **`Edit` tool** appending to an existing `.claude/artifacts/{ID}/decisions.md` **DENIED** and the file unchanged — and the same bytes on a quoted heredoc into the helper's stdin **allowed** and on disk byte-identical, `$200`, backticks, a backslash and a fenced code block intact (`MEASURE-35`, rows N03/N04/N08 and N07/P03/P04/P07). **A two-segment pipe into that stdin is allowed** (row T03), which is how a generator's output reaches `.claude/` without a redirect; **a brace group piped in is still refused** (row T02). Empty stdin writes nothing and returns 1, leaving any existing document untouched: a zero-byte `plan.md` that replaced a real one is worse than an absent one, and an absence is reported rather than papered over.

**Since 0.3.166 (MDF-196) the same four subcommands carry the artifacts whose write instruction lives in a SHARED skill or agent definition rather than in one command's own prose**, so the whole assisted lifecycle gets the route and not only `/deliver`: `plan.md` and `shared_risks.md` on a quoted heredoc (plan-feature Sections 8 and 9, `agents/planner.md`), the run record's `- tests:` and `- env:` lines on a `printf` pipe into `append-run` (`agents/builder.md` item 9 — a heredoc cannot interpolate the host port the same phase just read back), the three review scope manifests through `hooks/lib/review-scope.sh`, and the per-phase handover manifest through `hooks/lib/handover-manifest.sh` — both of which source this helper and call `write-*` themselves. **That last one is the discriminator worth remembering, because the two routes are not interchangeable:** an **unconditional** generator pipes its stdout into `write-item`, and a generator that legitimately produces **nothing** on some runs performs the write itself, because empty stdin is a caller bug by contract and a designed skip is not a bug — piping one would report an ordinary build's skipped re-check as a failure, and a reader who learns to ignore that line has learnt to ignore a real one.

**"No entry reaches it" was too strong, and the correction is the reason 5.5 declines the escape.** Measured 2026-09-09 on CLI 2.1.265 (MDF-187): with the bare tool name `Bash` in `permissions.allow`, a redirection into `.claude/` **lands** when the command is a **compound** one and stays refused when it is a **simple** one. A complete 2×2 on one directory and one extension, one variable: `{ echo 'x'; } > .claude/artifacts/{ID}/stats.jsonl` allowed and written to disk, `{ echo 'x'; } >> …` allowed and written, `echo 'x' > …` refused, `echo 'x' >> …` refused. Nothing about the brace group makes the write safer — the check does not inspect a compound command's redirect target — so **this is a hole, not a mechanism.** Do not wrap a refused write in braces to make it land: that is the "do not re-spell the command" clause above, and the hole is version-bound and can close in any CLI release.

### 5.4 Where a shape rule is enforced

`CONTRIBUTING.md` → "Bash command shape" binds skill and agent authors, and `tests/bash-command-shape.test.sh` fails CI on a forbidden shape appearing in `skills/` or `agents/`. A command a project's own configuration makes necessary is covered from the other side: `/sync-project` Section 5.1 derives a `Bash(<program>:*)` grant for every program named in `CLAUDE.md`'s declared commands and reports what it added, so a stack the framework has never heard of is granted because the project declared it, not because someone guessed it into the template.

### 5.5 Why the blanket `Bash` escape is declined

**The permissions documentation names one escape from the prefix-rule model: put the bare tool name `Bash` in `permissions.allow` and deny the few commands you want blocked from a `PreToolUse` hook. The framework measured it and declines it.** Priced by MDF-187 at 0.3.156, 27 rows on CLI 2.1.265 in a trusted throwaway clone, one variable, verdicts from `permission_denials` and from the file system for every write. **Do not re-price it without a new measurement**, and do not read "the docs describe it" as an argument — the docs describe what the rule form does, and none of the four grounds below is about that.

1. **What it buys is one self-check, plus three writes that land through 5.3's hole.** Of the shipped shapes still refused today that 5.1 does not already forbid, four stop prompting under the grant — but three of the four are brace-group writes into `.claude/`, allowed only for the parser reason 5.3 records. The single unqualified gain is one `sync-project` docs self-check whose failure an operator reads anyway.
2. **It does not reach the failure that is silent.** The step-marker idiom is a *simple* command, so it stays refused under the grant, measured in both arms. The one carrier here whose failure is deterministic and silent is exactly the one the escape does not fix.
3. **It contradicts the block it would join, and the contradiction is measured.** `templates/settings.json` retired its five bare *file*-tool grants at 0.3.139 (MDF-180) because a rule that is a tool name with no parentheses matches every use of that tool, and its only real effect is outside the working directory. The same is true of `Bash`: `cd backend && ls`, refused today, is allowed under the grant. A bare `Bash` would also make all 45 `Bash(…)` prefix grants in that block unable to change any verdict, which is the defect `tests/settings-inert-path-rules.test.sh` exists to catch.
4. **The denylist half faces the parsing problem that made the allow-list fail.** `permissions.deny` does still bind ahead of a blanket allow — measured, one variable, both directions — so the destructive set does not depend on the hook. But `deny` matches prefixes, and the shapes a blanket grant newly permits are precisely the ones no prefix parses: `$(…)`, a brace group, `cd` as a segment. A hook denylist over arbitrary shell misses silently, which 5.1's own opening paragraph ranks as the worst failure mode available.

**The consequence for the fenced generator scripts stands, and what it prices is a MEASUREMENT — never a lifecycle input.** A multi-line generator cannot be written without substitution and control flow, so `tests/bash-command-shape.test.sh` scopes itself to inline spans and those blocks are out of scope by design. On an unattended surface a fenced generator does not run. Where its output is a **statistics marker or a summary figure**, the step is reported as unmeasured per 5.3, and **that is a known cost, not an open question**: a run that delivered its work without a number beside it is a run that delivered its work.

**Where its output is a lifecycle INPUT, that pricing does not apply and the generator is not accepted — it becomes a script** (MDF-194). `review_scope.md` is what the reviewer is scoped to; `graph.md` is what a resume reads; `plan.md` is what `work_items.md` Section 8's idempotent-resume check looks for, and without it every resumed round replans from zero. The same refusal costs a measurement in the first case and **the work itself** in the second, and only the first was ever priced here. The route is 5.3's, and a **brace group** piped in is still refused (row T02), so a generator that is a fenced `{ …; } > path` block does not gain a pipe — **it moves into a script under `hooks/lib/` and the skill invokes that**. Whether that script's output then goes down a pipe into `hooks/lib/run-dir.sh`'s `write-*`/`append-*` stdin (measured allowed, row T03) or the script calls `run_dir_artifact` itself turns on one thing: whether the generator can legitimately produce nothing. **No lifecycle-input generator is left in `skills/`** — `graph.md` pipes, and at 0.3.166 (MDF-196) the three review scope manifests moved into `hooks/lib/review-scope.sh`, which writes them itself because two of its three subcommands have a designed skip arm, and the per-phase handover manifest moved into `hooks/lib/handover-manifest.sh`, which had to move whole because it computes `pwd`, the branch and the merge base and a **`$(…)` substitution is refused whatever else is in the command**. That last point is the one to carry: **a command refused on more than one count is not fixed by removing one of them**, and the residual looks exactly like a fix. Re-derive every blocker on the shipped command, never just the one a ticket named. **The test for which arm you are in is one question: would a later step read this file, or does it only ever get counted?**

### 5.6 Why the read fence is declined, and why setting it breaks 5.1's widening route

**`permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories: true` is not shipped, and a project must not add it.** The settings reference describes it as fencing reads to the working directories, which sounds like exactly what 5.1's fourth bullet asks for. Measured, it buys nothing there and it takes `permissions.additionalDirectories` down with it. Priced by MDF-180 at 0.3.139 (54 rows, CLI 2.1.263) and settled by MDF-188 at 0.3.157 (CLI 2.1.266), one variable per row, verdicts from `permission_denials` and from the model's own word against an inside-the-repo positive control. **Do not re-adopt it from the documentation**, and do not read "it is the documented way to confine reads" as an argument — the documentation is right about what the key does and silent about what it undoes.

1. **It changes no verdict in the direction you want it.** Every outside shape it was meant to fence — the Read tool, a sibling checkout, `cat`, `head`, a Write, an Edit — is **already refused** without it, once no bare file-tool grant is present (which is the shipped block from 0.3.139; see `templates/README.md`). Measured in `acceptEdits`, `auto` **and** `bypassPermissions`. The permission-modes documentation's "the prompt doesn't appear in non-interactive `-p` runs; reads there run as before" is false on this CLI, and that sentence was the fence's whole justification.
2. **It overrides `permissions.additionalDirectories`, which is the one mechanism 5.1's fourth bullet names.** One variable, both directions: a file inside an ordinary additional directory reads fine with the fence off, by the Read tool and by `cat`, and is refused with it on. So setting the fence removes the framework's own shipped plugin-cache coverage — the hook libraries, the materialized rule sources and the version probe all stop being readable, and the symptom is a command that stops rather than one that prompts. **The clause that used to stand here, “wherever that cache is not inside the *active* `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`”, was a live defect described as a hypothetical and it is fixed rather than restated:** on such a host the shipped entry named a directory the plugin was not in and every read of a plugin file was refused with the fence off as well. Measured at 0.3.167 and remedied by the second entry 5.8 records, so the fence now takes away coverage that is really there on every host.
3. **That override is not a re-trust requirement, which was the last way out.** Each `additionalDirectories` entry is listed in the workspace trust dialog, so the override might have been an artifact of a directory trusted before the entry existed. It is not: the fence-off twin carried the same entry under the same already-accepted trust and was **allowed**, so an entry added after trust takes effect without re-accepting anything. The trust state is identical in both arms of the pair, and a condition that is constant across both arms cannot explain the difference between them. Re-confirmed forward on CLI 2.1.266.
4. **What it would buy is a confirmation dialog, on the one surface that already has a human on it.** The remaining difference is attended: interactively an outside read prompts and can be approved, and with the fence it is refused outright. That is a real difference and it is the wrong trade — an approvable prompt in front of an operator, bought by disabling the widening mechanism every unattended surface depends on. **A guard that fires only where somebody is already watching, at the price of a mechanism that works where nobody is, is a downgrade.**

**Reaching outside deliberately stays per-path and stays a project decision:** `--add-dir <path>` at launch, `/add-dir` in a session, or `permissions.additionalDirectories` in a gitignored `.claude/settings.local.json`. `tests/settings-inert-path-rules.test.sh` Part 4 fails CI if any shipped JSON carrying a `permissions` object sets the fence.

### 5.7 How a plugin script is named: the pointer, never the placeholder

**Every model-emitted command that runs a plugin script names it `~/.mayker/mayker-dev/<path>`, unquoted.** `~/.mayker/mayker-dev` is a symlink to the root of the plugin version this session loaded. `hooks/plugin-root-link.sh` refreshes it at every session start, wired on `SessionStart` in the plugin manifest; it is the only writer, it learns the root from its own location rather than composing one, and it exits 0 whatever happens.

Four reasons, and the first three are measured rather than argued (MDF-195, CLI 2.1.267, trusted clone under `templates/settings.json` verbatim, one variable per row, verdicts from `permission_denials` **and** from the file system):

1. **The placeholder does not work outside a hook.** `bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/…/run-dir.sh" …` is DENIED and nothing lands (row `W01`; the path is elided here on purpose, because Part 6 of the suite scans this file too and prose about a failing form contains the failing form, `REPO-30`); so is the unbraced form with the CLI's own value (`W03`); so is `cat` of the same path (MDF-194 `R01`/`S03`). 5.1's last bullet has the two discriminators.
2. **The pointer works, and RUNNING a script through it needs no settings entry.** `bash ~/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/run-dir.sh mark-item …` is allowed and its marker line is on disk (rows `W02`, `W05`), and those rows were taken under `templates/settings.json` verbatim at 0.3.165, when `~/.mayker` was in no `additionalDirectories` entry at all: a program argument is not path-fenced, so this spelling never depended on a grant and still does not. **It is in an entry now, and for the other route:** since 0.3.167 the same pointer is what covers the plugin cache for a *read* on a host whose `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is not the default (5.8). Do not read that entry as the reason a Bash call works, and do not delete it on the grounds that a Bash call does not need it.
3. **It survives a plugin version bump.** The plugin cache holds one directory per installed version (`…/mayker-dev/0.3.132/`, `…/0.3.111/`), which is exactly why the shipped `additionalDirectories` entry stops at the parent. A call site cannot stop there: it would name one release and stale on the next. The link is repointed at every session start, so it names the version this session actually loaded.
4. **It survives a non-default `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.** The link lives under `$HOME`, not under the config directory, and the hook resolves the root from its own path, so a host running `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-second` gets a correct pointer with no per-host value anywhere in this prose.

**If the link is missing the failure is loud, and that is the point.** `bash: /Users/…/.mayker/mayker-dev/hooks/lib/run-dir.sh: No such file or directory`, exit 127, on the session's own tool output. Compare what it replaces: a refused command produces no output, no error, no file, and a run that reports success. The hook also prints one line into the session's opening context when it cannot write the link, which is the only thing it ever prints.

**The line between the two spellings is what a BASH COMMAND names against what a FILE TOOL is pointed at, and it is measured on both sides.** A Bash command may not carry the placeholder at all, because the permission analysis refuses it (rows `W01`, `W03`, `R01`, `S03`); a **Read tool** citation may, because the session resolves it to the real plugin-cache path and a Read there is **allowed** under the shipped `additionalDirectories` entry (row `Y02`). So a plugin file a session must *read* keeps its `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/<name>.md` citation: it already works, and changing it would add a second spelling for no verdict. **And the pointer is not for the plugin manifest**: `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` keeps `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in every hook command, because the CLI substitutes that placeholder itself before it runs a hook and a hook command never reaches the permission layer. `tests/bash-command-shape.test.sh` Part 6 fails CI on a plugin-script call site that reverts to the placeholder, on a quoted tilde, and on a corpus that has lost the idiom altogether.

**The caveat this section used to close on is resolved, and 5.8 is where it went.** Every read of a plugin file, through the placeholder or through the pointer, depends on an `additionalDirectories` entry that names the cache the CLI actually loaded from — which the single shipped entry did not do on a host whose `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is not the default. That is fixed at 0.3.167 by a second entry rather than by a spelling, because no spelling of a call site can reach it.

### 5.8 The plugin cache takes two `additionalDirectories` entries, and the second one is the pointer

**`templates/settings.json` ships both `~/.claude/plugins/cache/mayker/mayker-dev` and `~/.mayker/mayker-dev`, and neither is redundant.** The first names the plugin cache under the **default** config directory. The CLI loads the plugin from `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/plugins/cache/…`, so on a host that sets that variable the first entry covers a directory the plugin is not in and **every read of a plugin file is refused**: the seven always-on standards a skill reads straight from the plugin, the version probe and every `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/<name>.md` citation. The symptom is a command that stops rather than one that prompts, and on an unattended surface the read is simply never performed and the phase proceeds without the standard it was told to apply.

Measured at 0.3.167 (MDF-197) on CLI **2.1.267**, in the trusted throwaway clone `/private/tmp/probe` under this template verbatim, `claude -p --output-format json --setting-sources project` with stdin closed, one variable per row, verdicts from `permission_denials` and every reply asserted to be exactly the verdict word:

1. **The defect, one variable.** A Read of `…/mayker-dev/0.3.132/rules/testing_standards.md` under the **default** cache is **allowed** (row `E2`) and the same read under a `~/.claude-second` config directory is **DENIED** (row `E1`), with no entry at all also DENIED as the negative control (row `E0`). MDF-195's `Y02`/`Y03` pair, re-taken forward.
2. **An environment variable is NOT expanded in an `additionalDirectories` value.** `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/plugins/cache/mayker/mayker-dev` as the entry leaves the same read **DENIED** (row `E3`), reproducing MDF-173's frozen row `A4` on a current CLI. **So a config directory cannot be named in a committed settings file**, and the cheapest fix does not exist.
3. **An entry IS resolved through a symlink.** With `~/.mayker/mayker-dev` in the entry set the read of the real cache path underneath is **allowed** (row `E6`), which is the same resolution `Y01`/`Z01` measured on the accessed side. The pointer therefore covers whichever config directory the plugin was actually loaded from, with no per-host value in any committed file.
4. **A dangling entry is tolerated and the rest of the block still binds** (row `E9`). The pointer does not exist until `plugin-root-link.sh` has run once on that machine, and an entry naming a path that is not there neither breaks the block nor withdraws the other entry — which is also the row that keeps the default-cache entry in the set rather than replacing it.
5. **The fence resolves an entry at CHECK time, not at startup** (row `E10`). A session that began with the pointer aimed at the previous version repointed it mid-turn and the read landed, so the `SessionStart` refresh is early enough and a plugin update leaves no stale window.
6. **No mirrored `deny` ships, and that is measured rather than overlooked.** `permissions.deny` keeps `Edit(~/.claude/plugins/cache/**)` so the default cache stays read-only under `defaultMode: acceptEdits`. A second rule for the active cache would change no verdict: with that cache in `additionalDirectories` and no deny naming it, an **`Edit` tool call on a file inside it is still DENIED** and the file is unchanged (row `E7`) — an additional directory opens a **read**, not an edit. A grant or a guard that changes no verdict may not ship (`REPO-43` point 2), so the arm with the extra deny was not taken: it is moot by conjunction, recorded as a decision rather than predicted (row `E8`).

**The rejected alternative is measured, not unmeasured.** Deriving the resolved absolute path at `/sync-project` time and writing it into the gitignored `.claude/settings.local.json` works — the derived entry opens the read (row `E4`) and it opens it from the local file too (row `E5`) — and it loses on cost: a second output file for `hooks/lib/settings-permissions-reconcile.sh`, a per-host value that has to be re-derived on every machine, and a repo that is only correct after a sync run, against two static lines that are identical on every host and reach every existing repo through the entry-set heal the reconciler already performs.
